title: Cities that never sleep?
text: Night-time economies have become a measure of urban {{1}}, and cities compete to advertise how much happens after dark. Yet researchers studying night workers tell a more complicated story. The 24-hour city {{2}} on an invisible workforce of cleaners, drivers, bakers and security staff whose routines invert normal life. Working nights is associated with serious health {{3}}, from disrupted sleep to increased risk of certain diseases, and night workers {{4}} report feeling socially invisible: shops, clinics and banks all assume daytime hours. Some cities now appoint 'night mayors' to {{5}} for this workforce, extending transport and services into the small hours. Early evidence suggests the approach {{6}}: restaurants in one pilot city reported better staff retention after late-night bus routes were introduced. The lesson is an old one — a city's glamour depends on workers it {{7}} notices, and supporting them costs far less than {{8}} them.

gaps.explanation: 'depends on' — the preposition follows the verb.
'report themselves' — they report their own feeling; reflexive pronoun.
'speak for this workforce' — represent their interests.
'workers it rarely notices' — adverb of frequency.
'costs far less than ignoring them' — gerund after than.
